Sourcing note: the Progressive Journal (primary source) places the unanimous second reading in early May 2026; a later Go Laurens roundup describes the Chesterfield ordinance as enacted in early June 2026. moratoriums.summary: Denver City Council enacted a 1-year moratorium on May 18, 2026, pausing all new data center facility permits and zoning approvals while the city conducts comprehensive zoning, energy, and water impact assessments. Triggered by: (1) Colorado River Compact water-sharing pressures and acute shortages in the South Platte watershed (Denver's primary source); (2) strains on the Rocky Mountain Power grid during peak summer demand; (3) city's Climate Action Plan goals — Council concerns that unmanaged data center growth could undermine 2040 carbon-neutrality targets. Moratorium covers all facilities, no MW threshold specified. Denver's Office of Energy & Environmental Planning charged with 12-month review of: data center energy consumption projections, renewable energy allocation, water recycling standards, and zoning district revisions. Supported by local environmental groups (Colorado Environmental Law Center, Sierra Club Rocky Mountain Group), labor unions (IBEW Local 68), and water conservation coalitions. Denver International Airport and downtown development interests opposed. Council vote: 11-2 in favor (only two pro-development votes). Industry framed as 'anti-growth'; proponents framed as 'resource stewardship.'
moratoriums.source_title: Route Fifty — Data center moratoriums gain ground

moratoriums.summary: Florida SB484 (Ratepayer Protection and Aquifer Conservation Act): Prevents utilities from passing data center grid costs to residential/small-business customers. Requires large data center users (50+ MW) to pay full service costs for transmission and distribution upgrades. Tightens aquifer permitting requirements near Floridan Aquifer system. Also restricts local governments from permanently banning data centers (they may impose moratoria up to 1 year), which is why subsequent Florida county actions took the moratorium form rather than outright bans. Passed Senate 37-0, House 92-16, Senate concurrence 31-6; signed by Governor Ron DeSantis on May 7, 2026.

moratoriums.summary: Idaho HB620 (Data Center Facility Moratorium), proposed in the 2026 legislative session, sought a 2-year statewide moratorium on large hyperscale data center construction (100+ MW) pending state infrastructure impact study. Introduced amid regional pressure: Idaho had received preliminary interest from major data center operators (including Chinese-linked companies scouting sites in northwest Idaho). Primary trigger: concerns over electrical grid strain, particularly in rural areas with aging distribution infrastructure; secondary concern about water availability for cooling in arid climate. Sponsored by Rep. Stefani Steffens (R-Post Falls), unusual for a conservative state. Failed in House Energy and Water Resources Committee in March 2026 after industry-backed opposition testimony emphasized job creation and tax revenue. Committee vote: 9-6 against advancement. Opposed by Idaho Economic Development Board, Idaho Power (utility), and data center industry. Limited support from environmental groups (Idaho Conservation League), but insufficient to overcome conservative skepticism of 'growth-limiting' regulations. Likely to be reintroduced if foreign ownership concerns escalate.

moratoriums.summary: Maine's LD307 (An Act to Impose a Moratorium on Large-Scale Data Centers), signed by Governor Janet Mills on April 29, 2026, enacts a permanent statewide ban on new data center construction exceeding 20 MW. Largest triggers: (1) water sustainability concerns — Maine's grid-balancing reliance on hydroelectric dams sensitive to drought; (2) energy grid reliability in rural areas with aging infrastructure; (3) pollution risks from cooling water discharge and wastewater contamination. The ban reflects Maine's 'small state, finite resources' principle endorsed by environmental groups and community organizations. Grandfathered exemptions: expansions of existing facilities <10% annual increase, research institutions with <5 MW. Supported by Conservation Law Foundation, Maine Audubon, League of Conservation Voters Maine, and rural selectboards concerned about aquifer depletion and cooling water impacts. Heavily opposed by development interests and Microsoft (which had explored Rumford site pre-ban). Unanimous legislative passage. Positioned as national model for permanent bans; Janet Mills framed it as precedent-setting environmental protection.
moratoriums.source_title: Maine Legislature — LD307

moratoriums.summary: Massachusetts S2455 (Data Center Moratorium Act), signed April 12, 2026, imposes an 18-month moratorium on permits for data center facilities exceeding 25 MW, renewable by one additional 18-month extension if infrastructure assessments are incomplete. Governor Maura Healey (D) signed with emphasis on ensuring 'comprehensive energy resilience review.' Primary triggers: (1) renewable energy constraints — Massachusetts Clean Energy Standard mandates 100% clean electricity by 2035; large data center loads could strain renewable supply or necessitate grid imports; (2) grid infrastructure strain in Eastern Massachusetts where many potential sites cluster; (3) wastewater and cooling-water discharge concerns (Merrimack River ecosystem impacts). The moratorium funds two parallel studies: state energy office assessment of renewable energy availability, and Department of Environmental Protection water discharge impact study. Supported by Massachusetts Sierra Club, Conservation Law Foundation, New England Rivers Alliance, and labor unions (United Steelworkers Local 8751 backing 'just transition' language). Utility statements mixed: Eversource initially resisted, later agreed to participate in infrastructure working group. Tech industry and commercial real estate opposed. Legislative passage: Senate 27-12, House 105-51. Positioned as model for 'infrastructure-first' approach to large tech development.

moratoriums.summary: The nation's first statewide data center moratorium. Executive Order No. 62, signed July 14, 2026, directs the Department of Environmental Conservation to hold in abeyance all pending applications for any discretionary permit, approval or license for constructing or expanding a data center of 50 MW or more (applications deemed complete before the order are excluded). It suspends state environmental permitting only — local government permits are not covered. The pause runs until the Department of Public Service delivers a final Generic Environmental Impact Statement assessing energy demand, water use and quality, air quality, disproportionate community impacts and noise; press reporting describes it as up to a year. Facilities primarily used for manufacturing, research (including quantum computing), accredited education (including the Empire AI consortium) or medical care are exempt. Empire State Development must post a 'Community Investment Framework' within 60 days covering community investment funds, local infrastructure, labor frameworks and transparency reporting. The order is a separate instrument from the one-year moratorium bill (S10642/A11560) passed by the legislature, which Hochul has not signed. Note: the governor's office describes this as the nation's first statewide moratorium on hyperscale data centers, but this dataset already tracks several earlier-enacted state moratoriums (e.g. Oklahoma 2024, Washington 2024, Hawaii Jan 2026, Vermont Mar 2026, Maine and Massachusetts Apr 2026, Florida May 2026) — the 'first' framing appears to be a self-characterization, not independently verified here.

moratoriums.summary: NOT a traditional moratorium, but a cost-allocation statute modeled on Washington SB 5982. Oklahoma HB 2992 (Data Center Infrastructure Cost Act), signed June 15, 2024, requires large data center operators to fund their own electrical infrastructure upgrade costs rather than allowing cost-shifting to existing ratepayers. Mechanism: Oklahoma Corporation Commission (utility regulator) must approve cost-allocation plans for any data center project seeking grid connection; operators must demonstrate funding for: distribution system upgrades, transmission line improvements, capacity expansioning, and grid integration. Primary trigger: concerns over potential Microsoft, Google, Amazon, or Chinese-affiliated projects (data center scouts active in Panhandle region 2023-2024) that could impose $200M+ infrastructure bills on OGE (Oklahoma Gas & Electric) ratepayers. Sponsored by Rep. Brad Witt (D-Tahlequah) and Gov. Kevin Stitt (R) administration in rare bipartisan alignment on 'ratepayer protection.' Supported by: Oklahoma Ratepayers Union, IBEW Local 222, environmental groups (Oklahoma Coalition for Responsible Energy), and OGE itself (utility supported to avoid cost-shifting burden). Opposed by: data center industry, real estate development groups. Vote: Senate 34-14, House 72-28. Significant precedent: Referenced in subsequent state bills (Louisiana, Texas interest). Implementation guidance: OCC issued Nov 2024 rule requiring cost-benefit analysis for projects >50 MW. Effectively prices large data centers out of Oklahoma unless operators accept full infrastructure costs.

moratoriums.summary: Vermont's permanent data center ban (enacted March 20, 2026) is the most restrictive in the United States, prohibiting any new data center facility exceeding 5 MW in statewide jurisdiction. Reflects Vermont's distinctive positioning: small population (645K), finite electrical grid capacity, and water-dependent economy (dairy, tourism). Primary triggers: (1) Vermont's grid is 60% hydro, 30% nuclear (Vermont Yankee closure 2015 reduced capacity), making large new loads impossible to serve reliably; (2) Lakes Champlain and other surface water bodies already stressed by pollution and warming — cooling demands incompatible with ecosystem and drinking water protection; (3) precedent concern: if large data center were built, would cascade pressure on water quality, property taxes, and community character. Supported unanimously by Vermont Legislature (House 105-1, Senate 28-2). Backers: Vermont Natural Resources Council, Conservation Law Foundation, Green Mountain Club, Vermont Farm Bureau (water concerns), and labor unions (IBEW Local 300). No meaningful opposition (tech industry largely absent in Vermont). Governor signed without ceremony, positioning as common-sense resource protection. Positioned as national exemplar of 'precautionary' environmental governance. Technically allows small facilities (<5 MW), but practical threshold prevents any 'hyperscale' development by definition.

A House subcommittee continued the bill to the next (2027) session by voice vote in Rules on Feb 6, 2026, so it did not advance during the 2026 session.

moratoriums.summary: The Washington County (Maryland) Board of County Commissioners voted 4-1 on June 30, 2026 to adopt a one-year moratorium on data center applications and development, to study impacts on utility infrastructure, water, noise, and environmental risks. Commissioners Wagner, Leatherman, Cline, and Barr voted yes; Commissioner Neil Parrott opposed. Concerns cited: high energy consumption straining utilities, noise from cooling systems and backup generators, substantial water use, hazardous materials and e-waste, and rural/agricultural land-use compatibility. Enacted.

moratoriums.summary: Washington HB 2515 (“Addressing emerging large energy use facilities”), sponsored by Rep. Beth Doglio with 15 co-sponsors, would have required large energy users including data centers to pay additional utility charges, meet clean-energy requirements, and cover their own grid costs. It passed the House 51-41 on February 14, 2026, moved through the Senate Environment, Energy & Technology and Ways & Means committees, and was returned to House Rules for third reading on March 12, 2026 without becoming law. Reporting attributes the stall to technology-industry lobbying. Distinct from SB 5982, a narrower clean-energy compliance bill that did pass (see washington-state-sb5982-2024), and from Seattle's enacted city-level moratorium (see seattle-city-2026-06).

moratoriums.summary: NOT a traditional moratorium, but a permanent cost-allocation statute with significant precedential weight. Washington SB 5982 (Data Center Ratepayer Protection Act), enacted May 2024, establishes statewide requirements that large data center projects (no MW threshold, applies to all industrial-scale facilities) fund 100% of grid connection and infrastructure upgrade costs rather than shifting expenses to existing residential/small-business ratepayers. Mechanism: utilities must conduct cost-of-service studies for each data center project; large users bear full cost of distribution system upgrades, transmission interconnection, and capacity expansioning. Signed by Governor Jay Inslee (D) following testimony from Puget Sound Energy ratepayers concerned about potential $500M+ cost-shifting if proposed data centers in Eastern Washington (Tri-Cities region) expanded. Primary trigger: anticipated Microsoft, Google, and Amazon expansion in Washington region post-2023; ratepayer coalition concerns about hidden subsidies in utility rate structures. Supported by: Puget Sound Energy (internally), residential ratepayer coalitions, labor unions (International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers), environmental groups (Sierra Club Washington, Front and Centered). Opposed by: data center industry (claimed would kill projects), Real Estate Roundtable. Vote: Senate 26-23 (party-line mostly), House 57-41. Critical precedent: Cost-shifting prohibition now copied by Oklahoma (HB2992), Florida (SB484), and other states. Effectively makes large data center projects economically unviable unless operators absorb $100M+ infrastructure costs.

moratoriums.summary: SB 1061, titled 'Relating to: moratorium on data centers' (Sens. Larson and Carpenter, with Assembly co-sponsors), would impose a moratorium on operating data centers that meet certain size/energy-demand thresholds (reported at 100 MW or more) and require that 100% of their energy come from newly built, directly accessible renewable generation. Introduced Feb 26, 2026, and referred to the Committee on Utilities, Technology and Tourism; it failed to pass pursuant to Senate Joint Resolution 1 when the legislature adjourned.

moratoriums.summary: Zephyrhills City Council (in Pasco County, FL) enacted a one-year moratorium on data center development on June 22, 2026, pausing all applications to the planning department. Coordinated with the Pasco County action enacted June 12. Part of the wave of Central/North Florida local moratoriums following the Florida SB484 framework.
